utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just if we can pull up a photograph, actually. D226.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's just a photograph of the buildings. Do you recognise, where it says "ZM Knin," what that building is?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that the office where General Cermak was?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the office next door, where it says "IZM, ZP Split," do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that I recognise that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever go into the headquarters of the Split Military District?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Maybe it's there that I met General Gotovina on the -- in September, in the 5th of September, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sure. Just concentrating on the building, where it says "ZM Knin," you went in there how many times?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's more than ten times, but I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that it was a building with which had -- of great activity. There were many things happening in there.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recollect that there was a big dining-room and a public kitchen at the building?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Did you go into General Cermak's office?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a couple of times. And also there was a sort of a conference room, you know, when we were more people that were required to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Would it be fair to say that, in your dealings with General Cermak, you were able to notice that he was dealing with many different issues and things, not only military matters?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard for me to stay because I don't understand Croat, but there was a lot of activity taking place even while we were having our meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. That's all I'll ask you about on that matter. Let us now go to another matter that was raised yesterday, which was the occupation of camp at Civljane.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Actually, there are more matters on this I should cover, Your Honour. I'm sorry about that, but it's important that I cover some other matters relating to this. Let us go to 65 ter 3069. It's a document that was also produced yesterday, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's record of minutes of a meeting that you were present at on the 29th of August with General Cermak, Mr. Al-Alfi. If we go to page 2, right at the foot of page 2, Mr. Al-Alfi also deals with the issue of the stolen UN vehicles. You were present at this meeting, because it seems that the vehicles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, for the record, we have to identify exactly what's on our screen now. If you say it's 65 ter 3069, is that one of the documents admitted into evidence? I'm just trying to go through my list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This is among the four documents, I do understand, Mr. Tieger, where were not all the necessary follow-up, that they slipped in half, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- do not appear on the list. And, Mr. Registrar, do you have an exhibit number for it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. There haven't been any exhibit numbers assigned for these four documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please prepare that, then, Mr. Registrar, so that we have -- let's do it right now so that we have better basis to continue to work. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the four documents are as follows: 65 ter number 04162 becomes Exhibit P408; 65 ter number 03069 becomes Exhibit P409; 65 ter number 3544 becomes Exhibit P410; and 65 ter number 3531 becomes Exhibit P411.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were no objections against those four documents. In the absence of any objections P408, P409, P410 and P411 are admitted into evidence. And we have now on our screen 65 ter 3069 which is now P409.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, with regard to the document that is on the screen, we did raise an issue with regard -- concerning the interpretation -- the translation, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Translation, yes. I remember that. May I take it that for P409 that the draft translation, which is even an earlier stage than the unrevised translations, that it will be checked whether the translation is in every respect correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just to make that clearer, in connection with yesterday's discussion, we were going to liaise with the Defence because Mr. Misetic and Mr. Kehoe had concerns about a particular portion, as I understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least, could we get an explicit report to the Chamber, either by you or by both parties, so that we can strike it off our pending issues list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The document is being looked at as we speak, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The issue of those stolen vehicles was raised at the meeting with Mr. Al-Alfi, as we see on page 2, because, is it right, they still weren't returned to you despite the orders within the Split Military District?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had not been returned, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And General Cermak said he'd submitted it: "It is embarrassing for me. The answer is still in the negative. I will repeat my orders," and wanted details about the vehicles seen two days ago. That's on page 3. We have no need to clock that up. I just said out of fullness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the last document on this matter is 65 ter 1727.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's dated the 11th of November, 1995, issued from Split Military District, a warning regarding stolen UNCRO vehicles. Again, four vehicles stolen. A warning that the conduct was inappropriate. And on page 2, we can see that it was issued by General Gotovina to the troops but signed by General Ademi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can that be enter into evidence as an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 307, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D307 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: General Forand, I've just referred to those to deal with all information that is there so that no one says I missed something out or anything like that? I'm now going to turn to the theft of the engineer equipment which was high-value property of yours, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: High value, and required also for the dismantling of the observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We know from the exhibit you produced yesterday, Prosecution 391, which we can pull up on the screen, that you wrote, again on this matter on the 11th of August, to General Cermak about the theft of this equipment and giving great details in relation to the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I am just wondering. We are just entering now a new subject. I mean, quite a lot of questions have been asked to this witness, or at least documents shown to him, about if I could call it the internal follow-up of his complaints, where he apparently had no knowledge whatsoever about this follow-up. If we ask him one question whether he was aware of any internal follow-up on his complaints which was not addressed to him, and if his answer is no, then you might perhaps agree with Mr. Tieger on tendering into evidence from the bar table any correspondence. Of course, whether that correspondence reflect what is was done or not down, if the witness doesn't know, it is of no use to put that to him. Then at least we have these documents in evidence, and that the Chamber then has received the information that where this witness says, "My complaints remained without a response," that at least there is internal documents which deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, our difficulty is this, and I'm not doing it to be controversial, but when this witness is interviewed and his statements taken and go into evidence, none of this is put to him. And our problem is that we are facing evidence in this courtroom of a serious nature where the witness has not been briefed and put into possession of the information, and assertions are made about General Cermak --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. The only thing I'm addressing is that if this witness says, "I never received from Prosecution side, or from wherever, any information about internal correspondence on the matter," then, of course, you could put all the internal correspondence to him and say, "Have you seen it?" The answer is no. "Does it say this and this?" He reads the documents. He reads exactly what we read. That's it. So what it adds at this moment, I mean, we're not here to inform this witness about the complete documentation that does exist. We are here to hear from this witness what he can tell us about, what he knows about it. Apparently, these are matters - and I'm again referring to the internal communication in writing - where he has appears to have no knowledge whatsoever. So, therefore, it is for the Chamber important to receive the material. And if there's anyone who could tell us more about it, fine, we'll then hear at a later stage, but then at least the documentation in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. I understand Your Honour's point entirely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... it saves time --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- and guidance on the matter. But what it does go is to control; and, Your Honour, yesterday, heard evidence from the Prosecution about these matters. This wasn't done, that wasn't done by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I fully agree with you, that you say the internal documentation shows that it was different. But whether it is of any use to put it to a witness who says, "I have got no knowledge about that," then, of course, the document should speak for themselves. And if you give the documents to the Chamber, the Chamber will read them and we'll learn what is in these documents. And whether the witness goes home with a mother complete picture, yes or no, of course might be important for him, but it is not important for the determination the Chamber has to make. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why I'm asking you these questions is because you gave evidence yesterday about Mr. Cermak having responsibility, and the documents that I'm putting to you show that he couldn't even issue orders to get your equipment back. He tried to help you and he issued orders to the police and military police, but he could go no further within the -- within the system. He didn't have the command and control of these troops that you may have thought he had.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my view, you know, he had the command over those troops, and I was not aware of all the inside paperwork that have you shown this morning. It's the first time I have seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is my problem, because the witness on the previous line of questioning admitted, "Well, I didn't know he didn't have control over these troops to issue ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kay, it is more complex, I think. This witness has told us what his impression at the time was. You show him a number of documents he is not aware of, and what these documents exactly tell us, whether there was command and control, is still to be seen. I mean, this witness just can read the documents, just as the Chamber can read the document at this moment. If I go an order to A, B, or C, then this witness who has told us clearly that he had not insight in the command structure, whether by looking at the latter giving instructions to A, B, and C, whether that for all purposes excludes that he could have given orders to D, E, or F is of course a matter of a conclusion, where the witness says he is not fully aware of this. We will have to put everything together at the very end: This correspondence, internal correspondence, what the witness tells us, also, including that he was not aware of any of these documents. We could follow the same procedure: Give him five letters, six letters, ask him whether he knows about it, whether he was familiar with the issues dealt with in these correspondence. If he says no, then we have the documents. The witness can't add anything to that. And, of course, we then have to consider whether the witness, when he gave his impressions about what was within and what was outside of the command and control of the accused, whether he had sufficient material to form such an opinion. That's it. I think I have been clear enough on --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the direction the Chamber would like this to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I will do on this collection of documents, I will take up Your Honour 's suggestion. We can put them to the Prosecution, and see if they will agree such measures in relation to the two issues that I was going to deal with: Engineering equipment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What we even could do is if we have a list of those documents, we could invite the witness to just go through it and say give an answer to the first question, whether he has ever seen the documents and, second, whether he had any awareness of what he finds in those documents as well as; for example, investigations, orders, whatever. If so, he could tell us; if not, then we just leave it to the documents we have available at that time. That will then be part of the puzzle the Chamber will later have to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful for Your Honours' suggestions; and, of course, we are listening to them and we will certainly follow them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One matter in relation to this issue, which I can put into you, as it is a letter written by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'd like to see 2D03-0002.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's a letter from you, dated 14th of August, about the camp at Civljane. I was going to put in further documents on this, but I will put in a document that you actually wrote. And you can see this letter on the 14th of August that you were still concerned that the camp at Civljane was occupied, and you said: "I cannot accept that these soldiers, a few minutes from Knin, do not obey your orders." Did you have a telephone conversation with General Cermak about this matter?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't think I would have had the telephone conversation. If I am sending him a letter, I think that's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The matter of "a few minutes from Knin, do not obey your orders," had you been told by someone that his orders were not being obeyed? How did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite obviously, they were still in camp, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Had that been communicated to you, though, as a fact?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Kenyans Battalion was reporting, you know, that the HV soldiers were still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I am going to turn to another matter now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can that be admitted into evidence, before I do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D308, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D308 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in your statement of the 6th of June, 1997, Prosecution Exhibit 331, page 19, line 19, you were referred to broaching subjects with General Cermak and concerning continued human rights violations. You said in this statement: "I never received an adequate answer. He always denied it. No, it did not happen, no, they were not responsible. It was Chetnik terrorists who did it in order to put the blame on the Croats," and what have you. And what I want to do now is actually refer to you a series of documents which show that is an inaccurate reflection of General Cermak's position to you concerning crimes being committed, General Forand. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would you agree that, in fact, he did admit crimes were being committed and that statement in your interview is inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was accurate. It happened couple of times where initially he was putting the blame on the Chetniks, you know, about the activity that was taking place for that. Eventually, this sentence, you know, was no longer part of the discussion we've had. But, initially, he was blaming it on the Chetniks. And when I say, you know, that I never received an adequate answer, if you look at all the letter that was sent to General Cermak raising the looting, the burning, and those other activities, they were carrying on. So, for me, when I say that, that's the fact that I never received an adequate answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's just look at that because it may be important, I don't know, to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But it's 11th of August, 1995, 65 ter 580. 11th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you wrote it him then on the 11th of August, you refer in the first paragraph to a meeting concerning his honest efforts to control the situation and you protested the activities. It's right, he was not denying, even then, that crimes were happening of which you were complaining? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Actual meeting, that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can that be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm almost certain it's in evidence, Your Honour. It was raised yesterday, to the best of my recollection, and was part of the package. It may be part of a sitrep appended to a larger document and may not have turned up for that reason. But I think we have a duplicate. I'm looking for it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would look for it, and then respond. Meanwhile, you can continue, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There are certainly duplicates of this letter in the 65 ter list. Let's go to D56 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we leave this document, I believe it is P363.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is the case, we actually must have a double, because that appears on the list as 0576; whereas, it was called up under number 65 ter 580. But, for the time being, I will check on P363, whether it is the same document. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Next document is D56, 18th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It a meeting that was held, and the notes of this meeting were sent to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "During the meeting, I brought to the attention of General Cermak our concern about continuing reports of houses and farms set on fire, looting. Asked measures taken from his side to stop such acts. General Cermak shared the concern with us, expressed his unhappiness about its continuation. He promised tough action against those who commit such abilities, and then gave an explanation: 'It may be carried out by civilians who return to the area and seek revenge.'" Another admission, would you agree, of crimes that were being committed?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to Prosecution Exhibit 374.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I meanwhile can clarify that the letter that was shown, 11th of August, is the fifth page out of nine in P363. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. P374, if we turn to page 3, paragraph 6, another sitrep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is the one we've referred to already where you have written, or someone in your team, "his area of responsibility is vast." I've showed it to you in the other document where the crimes were referred to: "He responded by attributing acts to bandits in army uniforms." He said: "Sincerely regretted. Such acts were contrary to the policy of the government of Croatia." You agree an admission of those crimes?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, you said, in your interview, that he was always denying it, and I'm saying again, and I have got several documents here that we can go through, where he actually admitted that there were crimes. There was --

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He admitted there was looting, burning, what was being put.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. The word "denying," that maybe I should not have used in my statement. To me, what I wanted to say was the fact that it was reported and nothing was being done about it .

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. Would that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, it is also fair, I think, to then -- you're focussing very much on page 19 of the witness statements, and then lines 17, where it says: "Every time." Of course, on that same page, we find: "He responded that he could not control some of these things that were going on." So, therefore, on the same page, we find a reference to repeated denial, but also a reference to admission that these things went on. And since you're focussing so much, I think it is fair to the witness to put that he might not have been fully consistent in his statement in this respect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you would agree with that - I've got more documents here, and I don't want to bear on the patience of the Court by going through them - where he is quite plainly is saying these crimes are happening?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I might adopt Your Honour's suggestion in relation to that, and put in just a little schedule so that those documents which save court time are referred to, to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, that is an agreeable procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. We're very receptive to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is one document, however, that I do want to refer to specifically, because it was dealt with at great length in your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is the letter of the 3rd of September, 65 ter number 1922. I apologise for not having the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, that's because of duplicates in the system. And if we could focus on the bottom of the page, not that part actually. In the Croatian, if we could focus on the signature on the bottom of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that's D145.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is the "name me one crime" letter that you referred to yesterday. Do you recollect it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you've got the bundle of correspondence from Mr. Cermak to you. And you have -- in the break, have you been able to flick through and see the letters that he actually -- that he wrote?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How they were written, the length of the letter, what was said?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I have seen all of that. And as I mentioned, you know, if it was addressed to me, I would have received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is only one which was in Croat which I didn't understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and it was not translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. That's just within the system and the system will correct that. But it is there for completeness so that nothing was missed out, and it comes from an electronic base that I will mention no more about.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This letter was written on the 3rd of September. You saw, on the 5th of September, in Knin, General Gotovina and with him Mr. Cermak's deputy. Do you recollect?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recollect seeing General Gotovina on the 5th; and after that, I think there was a meeting with General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Should be -- we'll stay where we are, rather than moving around too much. But do you recollect in the sitrep we saw yesterday about that meeting on the 5th of September with General Gotovina that there was another person present who was General Cermak's deputy?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, yeah. In the sitrep, I think his name is mentioned, but I don't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That was the Gojevic I mentioned to you before. Remember we were looking at the appointment today?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you corrected Mr. Tieger when you looked at the letter written by Brigadier-General Janvier?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, where he was associating that General Cermak was at the meeting with General Gotovina, which was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which was not the case. Do you recollect that at this time, at the beginning of September, that Mr. Cermak was not in Knin --

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- between the 1st of September and he returned on the 7th of September?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Did you look at this letter here, dated the 3rd of September, and consider it as being a different letter in style than the ones you'd previously received from General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on what I seen during the break which I had not remember those letter and based on the other letter, yes, it was different. And as I said yesterday, I was a little bit surprised by the content of that letter, based on all the other letters that I have been sending to General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Based on what he said to you in your meetings about crimes and what was happening, we've looked at it, he had admitted things were happening. And as you said, you had a very cordial relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would you agree that it didn't seem his style?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say that I didn't question. I was, like I say, surprised by the content of the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It has got his name at the bottom, but did you ever look at the signature at the bottom to see who signed it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Because when I get the letter, it's the translation that I receive. I don't get the original --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the sense that it has been translated by the translator that was at my headquarter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm told to correct the transcript. I can't say when the witness said yes. Perhaps Mr. Cayley who is observing it may, because I can't see the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's line 23 on page 62, the answer give the witness is "I can't say," and I heard him say, "Yes, sir."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then put the question again to him and see what his answer is. The question, Mr. Forand, was: "Based on what he said to you in your meetings about crimes and what was happening, we've looked at it, he had admitted things were happening. And as I said, you had a very cordial relationship with him." What was your answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is rather complex because it refers to both to meetings and that you've looked at it, that he admitted things, that the relationship was very cordial. That is quite a number of subjects in one question. Whether the witness said "yes" or "I can't say," in view of the complexity of the question, perhaps you split it up, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: My mistake. I was trying to do it in a short way. It seems never to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You previously agreed you had a good working relationship with Mr. Cermak. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He treated you with respect. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was very civilised, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And he accepted to you that crimes were being committed?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He had accepted that it was a problem in the region?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And would you agree that this was not in the same style of his manner of communicating with you?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it was not the same style. That's why I said I was surprised when I received that letter. But I never queried or it never crossed my mind that he would not have signed it, because as I said what I received was the translated portion, and I only see from who was signed it without the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that, looking at the signature, if I have been able to decipher if it was from him or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you appreciate that at the meeting on the 5th of September with General Gotovina, that General Cermak's deputy, Major Gojevic, was there because General Cermak was not in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Would you usually call or have a meeting with the deputy of General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that I ever went to a meeting if it was not General Cermak that was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked for admission of a 65 ter document 1922, because the one that is in the court system of D145 does not have this translation with the signature -- the original with the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D145 is presented as an English original, and seems to be a translation of that same letter, but with it seems some -- it might be of Mr. Al-Alfi, at least, on the date 5th of March, 1998. So someone has recognised that document. The typewriting is also different from the English translation of the original. So, for that reason, we can't just consider 1922 to be the same as D145. Therefore, any objections against the tendering of a document which apparently has the same content, because the language of the translation and D145 appears to be literally the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I had been about to raise the same point, and there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D309, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D309 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just the last matter on this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware that Mr. Cermak had been in the Croatian media condemning looting and crimes in the region?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That now deals with those matters. Your Honour, we took an early break, I recollect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And as a matter of fact, I would like to have, then, the second break earlier as well. That will be within five to ten minutes from now, if that is a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next matter I want to deal with is the issue of the displaced persons about which you gave evidence yesterday. We've already dealt with statements made by Mr. Cermak at the UNCRO camp on the 7th of August. I questioned you about that earlier today. That was on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we look at Prosecution Exhibit 359 and turn to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is your meeting with General Gotovina, paragraph 3, where the matter of the war criminals was raised by him at that meeting on that day. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you recognise, at the time, that the issue of anyone that was in your camp, sheltering, who had committed war crimes in previous conflicts was of great concern to the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you recognise that that was part of the agreement between the UN and the Croatian government that Mr. Akashi had signed?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that part, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. I want to have a look at that issue, as it's been a matter raised in this trial against Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to P388.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And Mr. Cermak, on the 8th, is writing and asking for the list of refugees. And on page 2, we've already referred to the identity of any men between the ages of 18 and 60. Did you know that it was -- that the matter of people being aged between 18 and 60 was the category taken because of the mobilisation of people -- of men within that age bracket for military service?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn now to 65 ter 1148, page 2 of that document, paragraph 1 of page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That refers to negotiations that you were having with General Cermak and progress was unable to be achieved, and that shortly General Cermak will not - there is an suggestion - will not have a say in this matter, and it was a matter as to who would assume real responsibility and decision-making powers. Did you appreciate that General Cermak was acting as a conduit on behalf of his government dealing with you on this issue?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you, yourself, was acting as a conduit on behalf of the UN authorities. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can go to 65 ter 1145 and page 3 of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, also for the previous document, could you also for the links that are supposed to be possible on the transcript give the P number, if it has a P number. If not, then it needs an exhibit number to be assigned it. We were talking about 65 ter 1148, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It has not been admitted yet, Your Honour. May I admitted that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D310.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D310 is admitted into evidence. And so now we move to 65 ter 1145 -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: P42. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I thought the other one was a duplicate, and that is why we stopped in our stride in relation to the other matter. It does get a little confusing at times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, if we are talking about 65 ter documents, if it ever comes to that, that either the Appeals Chamber or historians will look at these transcripts, they have to find their way through this material, and then we have to know whether it is an admitted exhibit or whether it's just a document which was once uploaded in an e-court system. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We're looking at page 3 of this document, P42, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is an HRAT report from Mr. Flynn, with whom you were liaising on this issue. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I was working with Mr. Al-Alfi, and I think Flynn was working for Al-Alfi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And the matter of the modalities of interviewing had yet to be agreed between the parties. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was some on- going discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For quite a time between --

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- you as a conduit and General Cermak as a conduit. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that instance, it was more the responsibility of Al-Alfi than myself. He was the one that was communicating with Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the moment for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. We will have a break and we will resume at 25 minutes to 1.00. Mr. Kay, is it your intention to provide any of these bundles to the witness so that he can just go through it, and if he has anything that is familiar to him or if he wants to add anything to what he sees, to give him an opportunity to do so. If we hear from him, then we will deal with the specific exhibit. If we do not hear from him, then it will be tendered from the bar table; and as we already understand, there will be no objection. Yes. Mr. Forand, we're spoiling your breaks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Hopefully, it will result in finishing your testimony this week, which the Chamber is very much determined that should happen. We have added all the times of Mr. Kay, Mr. Kehoe, et cetera, all the times. That brings us to approximately the remaining three days. If you take off approximately 10 per cent of that, then, Mr. Tieger, would you have some time for re-examination. If you say, No, I would need seven hours for that, the Chamber would like to know about it. But if it would be limited to half an hour up to 40 minutes, then we could conclude the testimony of this witness this week. That's what the Chamber urges the parties, and also the Defence teams amongst themselves, to agree on, on how to schedule that exactly. If you don't reach an agreement, of course, the Chamber will assist you, help you out. We resume at 25 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties have had a brief conversation with the senior legal officer about the way in which we proceed at this moment and have expressed some doubt as to whether the guidance the Chamber gave would lead us in the right direction. I'm not going to say too much about it, but the witness, at the time, has made observations and has translated these observations into, sometimes, conclusions. Now, the parties are establishing, at this moment, that the witness may not have had full information, that there's documentary evidence which may have been unknown to the witness, and that if wee have known, he might have adopted different conclusions. Now the Chamber of course is, first of all, focussing on what the witness observed, and the Chamber is not inviting the parties to see whether the witness would change his mind on the basis of documents that are put to him, because the Chamber is mainly and primarily interested in what the witness saw. And, of course, sometimes you can't avoid conclusions, as not specifically referring to this witness, if someone enters a house in uniform and then comes out, and suddenly the house is set fire, if then the person says, "I can't imagine an other thing and that person must have put that house on fire," then that is still a conclusion, and still, of course, for the Chamber to consider how compelling such a conclusion its, because it is finally the conclusions of the Chamber that count and not the conclusions of the witnesses primarily. And starting from this point of view, to see whether the witness would change his opinion on the basis of documents he could just had a glance on and without knowing, doesn't really assist. More important is that the Chamber is aware of the type of documentation which apparently has not been available to the witness, and it is important to establish that, and whether that would lead to any conclusions different from the conclusions the witness had on his mind is primarily for the Chamber to decide. Now, if the parties would like to test with one or two documents whether these are really documents the witness has no knowledge about, then the Chamber would not oppose that. But to go through a whole series of documents for of the first to learn that he isn't aware for the second, the third, the fourth, the fifth, the sixth, the same doesn't assist the Chamber. However, the Chamber is interested in looking at those documents because to the extent the authenticity is not contested by the Prosecution which has not been done, which wasn't the case until now, then the Chamber, at least, when we have all of the evidence before us, is aware that there is documentary evidence which deals with matters apparently related to what a witness testified about, but also unknown to the witness. That is, again, some short guidance. And if there is any specific document on which the Defence would want to focus, fine; but not through the whole of series and receiving the same very short answers, "no," "you're right," you know the kind of answers. If this would further guide the parties, then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful for the guidance, and I know that in the spirit of fairness that the Court is giving it in. Our position from the Defence side is that allegations are made, and we believe he was served a partial picture, part of the story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Give us the remainder of the picture, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am trying through the documents. All the subjects that have I raised in cross-examination are exact topics that Mr. Tieger covered in his four hours yesterday, in a very rapid form, which on first blush gives one flavour of the case. But from our position, and it is for the Court to accept or reject this, from what I'm submitting to you is that there is documentation in here that provides an entirely different picture. We know this is going to be a long case, it's a complex case, and we're doing it to help the Court, as soon as possible, to be aware of substantial issues of disagreement which I know the Court wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's no problem. The only thing we're talking about is whether the other part of the picture or the other picture in which way it will be presented in this Court, and what is the use of trying to also inform the witness that he might not have had the complete picture. It's for us to know whether the witness had a complete picture when he gave his statements, rather than to send him home fully informed about all of details. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I just say one matter, Your Honour. My reservation or thought on Your Honours' guidance is this: Many of the witness statements, not the least of which is General Forand, expresses certain conclusions based on certain facts. That is in the record; and, certainly, the Office of the Prosecutor has done -- has not taken any steps to redact those conclusions from those statements. I suppose, based on Your Honours' comments, are we to conclude that that is going to given no weight, given the fact that it is a conclusion as opposed to an observation on a fact? And I say that keeping in mind a rule that Mr. Tieger reminded me of sometime ago, Rule 90(H)(ii), concerning the cross-examination of a witness and the duty of counsel to put the witness -- counsel shall put to that witness the nature of the case of the party for whom the counsel appears which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness. And I think that that certainly, from our case and I don't want to speak completely for my learned friend, but I think that is what we're talking about. And in the best efforts to try to give the full picture to the Chamber, that is what we were trying to do, especially since these conclusions, not just by General Forand but by others, are sitting out there in these 92 ter statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, that is an issue, I must say, the way in which this rule is applied, that you have to put to the witness if you go -- first of all, let's not forget that is not for cross-examination, in general, but especially if you go beyond what was presented in examination-in-chief, as far as I'm concerned. But let me just check the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is 90(H)(ii). The one I just quoted from was (ii).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is not just in cross-examination, but cross-examination of a witness who is able to give evidence relevant to the case of the cross-examining party. That's, of course, not all of the cross-examination, but it is fine. I mean, it's not difficult to do that, I would say, and does not necessarily need to present all the documents to the witness. If you say, "Witness, it is the case of the Defence that when you, on the basis of your observations, you would have drawn wrong conclusions because you were unfamiliar a lot of other documents," and then ask him, "Were you aware of the existence of these documents?" Then put one or two to him, that is fine. But to go through 20 documents and then to find out that he has no knowledge of any of these documents, that, of course, take as lot of time. We could, if you want to, present that documentary evidence to the Chamber, in support of the Defence position that the witness was not fully informed about everything that happened and what he observed or the conversations he had. It gives limited information and not the full information. Then, of course, if we see these 20 letters, we'll know that he was at least short of 20 letters of information. What then the meaning of those letters is, is, of course, the next question and not for the witness to determine, because whether there are other documents that would contradict or other evidence by other witnesses who contradict those letters or support those letters is not for the witness to determine, mainly because what we would then invite him to do, where he is perhaps not blamed, but at least it's put to him that he had no full information when he made these statements, we would then invite him to do the same thing; that is, with a little bit more of information, to again draw conclusions or give states. Whereas, it is finally for the Chamber, at the very end, having heard all of the evidence, to see what the right conclusions are. Mr. Tieger, you were on your feet, but you desperately sat down again. Was there anything more?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not so desperately, Your Honour, just courteously, I hope. No. I was only going to suggest that perhaps we could move forward with this witness's testimony. I don't know the extent to which the discussion implicates issues which any of the parties feel will arise in the course of the remaining examination. I had the impression, having participated in the discussion with the senior legal officer, there was concern about possible future situations in which the guidance, if applied in a certain way, might hamper the Defence, but I don't know that the witness needs to participate or sit by while we participate in discussions of hypothetical circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If any such issue arise in the future, the Chamber is always open to discuss it, to explain what and why it wishes to proceed in a certain way, and will carefully listens to the questions. Mr. Kehoe, you added one question of whether the conclusions of no weight will be given to it. Well, no weight, it, of course, all depends on what type of conclusions there are. To say no weight whatsoever, of course we consider it in the totality of -- sometimes, we might give no weight at all to the conclusions; and sometimes, in the totality of the evidence, we might say, well, this is what the conclusion should it be. So, therefore, the Chamber will also carefully check to what extent, if a witness draws any conclusions, whether the Chamber, on the whole of the evidence, would draw similar conclusions, and then whether we give weight to the conclusions of the witness or whether we draw our own conclusions, would then appear to be the same or different ones from the witness is a bit of a semantical issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, and I don't what to belabour the point, but the witness is here and maybe we can address it in another form. That, of course, is the crux of the matter for the Defence, that those are out there. And the issue of if you had this other information, I'm not talking about General Forand at this point, but just hypothetically any witness, would that call into question the conclusion that you gave on page 3, paragraph 44 of your statement, and that is the issue that concerns the Defence most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that. I can say the following: That in one of the previous cases on which I have been sitting, the parties, especially on the 92 ter statements, always had a huge battle on what line to strike, whether there was a bit of a conclusion in it, or where it came to opinions. And I think it took a great effort to redact these statements in every respect. I observed that this has not happened before this Chamber. I would not encourage the parties to do it because it leads to lengthy conclusions where the parties do or do not agree on what exactly is a conclusion or just a logical consequence of the factual observations by the witness. It took us a lot of time. I don't think that it changed that much. But, finally, the parties stopped having similar battles when I had indicated that if the parties could not agree on striking certain portions, yes or no, that they're invited at 7.00 in the morning or at 10.00 at night to further discuss the matter in my presence, and then I would give them the guidance what could be struck or not. I'm telling this because the parties should be aware that not being a jury, but being a Bench of professionals, that we have many, many years of training to make clear distinctions between what are conclusions, what are opinions, and what are facts observed, and also which conclusions are so compelling that it's just impossible to desist from them and others which are far less compelling and which the Chamber might not adopt on the same basis as the witness may have done, which does not exclude for the possibility that the Chamber draws similar conclusions on the basis of the evidence as a whole. Mr. Forand, I take it that you have never been subject to these kind of discussions which are mainly about the law of evidence, which keeps lawyers busy for centuries already, and especially since lawyers come from different areas of the world. It keeps them divided also. I can't instruct to you forget about it. But if you didn't like it, that meets full understanding from all of us, and I speak on behalf all. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the spirit of that, General Forand, I'm going to skip certain documents in a chain which would have dealt with the full issue of the 55 displaced persons inside UNCRO battalion locations. In particular, you remember outside the UNCRO compound in Knin, you had the other battalions spread around the region, and some of those had become harbours of people where they had come to stay. You remember that particular issue?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let me turn to a document which is P369 which is one of your sitreps. While it is coming up, it wasn't only you involved in this. It was Mr. Flynn, Mr. Al-Alfi, and other agencies, all dealing with this issue. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which issue are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The 55 -- or 50 to 55 displaced persons in your other compounds.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was involved because it was my troops that had those people, but obviously the thing that pertained to the IDP situation or solution was now in the hands of Mr. Al-Alfi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And for the Court's reference, there's a document, D56, from the other agencies dealing with this matter, and I say that, as an Exhibit, to link it for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to page 3, this document says: "General Cermak and Senior ..." -- what is SLO-SS, Senior Liaison Officer?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Lieutenant-Colonel Tymchuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was agreed that all refugees now in unit locations should be relocated to Knin. General Cermak showed a great deal of flexibility and cooperation in compromising to finally resolve this long-standing and difficult issue. Once agreement was reached, rapid action followed. There was a conference, there were joint teams. All refugees will be offered the option of moving to Knin under UN protection or returning to their homes. And that's what was the of the object of the exercise, was to get these people into Knin so that the whole plan of dealing with these people could be progressed forward. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It was also in the view of eventually when they would be able to move out, you know, of Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. There is link document to this that's not an exhibit from HRAT which I will skip, and we will go straight to a letter from you to General Cermak, 2D03-0012. I'm going to the end of the story, missing out bits in between. You understand?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's a letter dated 19th of August. It's to you from General Cermak. It hasn't been seen by the Court before, and it's a letter of appreciation assistance in moving displaced persons: "Dear General, thank you very much for your assistance in escorting 51 displaced persons under UN protection from camps throughout Sector South to my headquarters in Knin yesterday." You refer to him giving support to the UN, professional response of Croatian army military police, your liaison staff. You express sincere gratitude, and you look forward further opportunities for close cooperation in a common purpose about the transfer of those persons from the UNCRO camp to destinations of choice in the near future. Is that right that General Cermak was extremely helpful on this issue?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As described in that letter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a very minor matter, but Mr. Kay inadvertently began by saying, "It is to you from General Cermak," and I think he wanted to indicate the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, yes, as we can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that was, again, one of your problems that he and you had to face during that time in August, and from which -- and in respect of which both of you were working together. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we have that made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. Tieger? Then, Mr. Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D311, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D311 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next matter which was raised in detail yesterday was the issue of those who were to be interviewed as suspects for war crimes, which was a big sticking point between the Croatian government and the UN. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, have I here a whole massive section of documents, but I don't intend to take you through every one, and I will follow the Court's guidance on it. We've dealt in part with that by referring to the fact that D28, the Akashi-Sarinic agreement, contained provisions to deal with this particular issue, as you recollect?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just to set the terms of reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kay, it is the second time that you raise this issue. As a matter of fact, from what I see in that agreement, it does not deal with people being interviewed as suspects. What it deals with, as far as I can see - and I think this is it paragraph 3, but I'm now talking from the top of my head - that is says that everyone is free to leave but not those who have committed, and I think even war crimes, not crime, but war crimes. It doesn't say anything about starting investigations on those who have committed and who have not. So, if you say interviews are dealt with, that is, in my view, if not a whole step, then at least half a step too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We agreed today that the modalities had to be sorted out. It was appreciated that the document did not deal with the precise way to resolve this issue. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. If I remember well, I think General Cermak wanted to interview those people outside of the camp, and the direction I got on that is that would not be the case. It would be inside, and those were the discussions that were ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Do you agree on this issue, as on the other issue, that General Cermak was acting as a conduit for his government in making representations on this issue?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: For this issue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the positions that he held in relation -- or the points of view he put forward eventually, both you and he agreed, had to be resolved at a higher level between the UN command in Zagreb and the government of Croatia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not aware of him, you know, that who he was going to in order to get the direction. Me, I was aware that I had to go back to Zagreb on the UN side to get their direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it correct that, in fact, members of the Croatian government became involved directly in this matter to resolve the issue?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm afraid then we have to look at some documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can imagine that if the witness says, "I don't remember," that is different from "I don't know anything about it." So, therefore, you can see whether the documentation could help the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour, and I am trying to follow the spirit of Your Honours' ruling in the best way that I can. Let's just start with a document here, D56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from dealing with the witness, is this a matter in dispute, Mr. Tieger, that is also, I mean, whether the witness knows anything about it, whether he could further assist us and whether it is an issue which is in dispute. And the issue apparently being at what level both, if I could say, interlocutors even if would be in writing at what level decision-making primarily took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't believe so Your Honour. I don't -- I obviously don't know precisely what point with respect to who got involved counsel has in mind, but the general matter that has been raised, no, it's not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If this serves as additional guidance, please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to Your Honour for that intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 3 of this document, which was a document that was sent to you as well, and I'm just referring to the bottom half of the page. A list was needed of the displaced persons because people had to know who was within the camp, isn't that right, General, that list had to be compiled?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we see in the last paragraph: "From our discussion, we also understood from General Cermak that the idea of carrying out investigations ... may be limited to a very small number of displaced persons, probably between 10 and 20 ..." And in this regard, General Cermak pointed out that the Croatian authority would ask for those people to be handed over. And were you aware of the fact that General Cermak thought that this was going to actually be a very small number of people that were to be considered or investigated, to be handed over as war criminals to the Croatian justice system?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember is that - I don't know exactly because I don't know when that letter that I have in front of me was signed - at one point, there was 62 persons initially that were considered. And at the meeting, General Cermak said probably that number would be lower. But this letter, I don't remember, you know, this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have skipped up the chain, but it is the 18th of August, this, when it first started to come together as a concrete problem.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would you agree that, how I put it in that way, that it took a few weeks to bring it up as an issue as to what was going to happen? It wasn't immediately dealt with from the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If I remember well, I think there was a request initially from General Cermak to provide the list from the 18 to the 60. I suppose we -- I don't remember, but we must have provided that list. So that started early on. But, yes, I agree with you, it took a long time to resolve.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And that was something that took from this date of the 18th of August until the final movement of the people on the 16th of September. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. There was also, is it not right, a great degree of correspondence over the actual identities of the people, the listing of the people within the camp, 687 persons being submitted on one list and then a later list with more people being submitted on the list? Do you recollect that as a particular issue?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, because I think it was Mr. Al-Alfi that was compiling that list, so I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. I've no need to stick on that. On the 21st of August, again, there was a discussion about this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 65 ter 1220. This is no cover sheet. It goes straight in the document, so it is the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we see that General Cermak asked to see you about this matter of the displaced persons. And in paragraph, 2 he refers to the fact he had been provided with a list of 687 persons. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Out of a population of 731. Then General Cermak indicated he had a list of 74 persons under suspicion of war crimes, which he said he thought the list was too long and could be shortened, which is what you mentioned before. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I mentioned the number 62, but, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to the chain of documents on this, that's all we need to look at. May this be admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection. I'm just checking to see if it was a portion of a larger document already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, could you assist Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's one that we got off the list as 65 ter 1220, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it is part of P403.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there's no need further to -- it is now on the record where to further find the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Then the process was the list of the 74 suspects were required to be handed over. Is that right General Forand, as you recollect it?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that particular point, but it would make sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the UN side were looking for details as to the type or the nature of the allegations that were to be raised against these particular individuals. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From what I remember, the direction that we had received, or that Mr. Al-Alfi had received, was they need to have some certain proof against those individual. Once these proof would have been presented to Mr. Al-Alfi, he would go back to the UN in Zagreb, present it to the lawyer, and they would agree or not, you know, if it was sufficient information in those description.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we look at a document dated the 21st of August, 1995, 2D03-0049.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: While this is coming, I will just introduce it. This is a document of the 21st of August which came from the security and information service, SIS, and was sent to General Cermak, and was the list of the 72 people who were those under discussion as to what the allegation was in relation to those people. And we can see on page 1 their names, and on the right-hand side a description of the nature of the allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's a four-page document. We've no need to look into it any further unless anyone wants to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But the point of presenting it is to say, did you see this document, the one that came from the Croatian side, which was to help identify in your camp those who were suspected of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember seeing that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you personally have any dealings in relation to that aspect of the issue as to the nature of the crimes and the particular individuals, or was that someone else within your UN people in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my point of view, it was Mr. Al-Alfi that was taking care of that. I never got involved in those discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because it was outside your responsibility.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document be admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D312, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D312 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recollect if there was an issue as to whether the UN would receive the information in a particular form --

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- whether service of the notice by the Croatian authorities had to be done in a particular way and the protocol associated with it? Do you recollect that particular issue?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Like I said, you know, I was not involved and it's not something that I got involved at all in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we look at P374.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This document of the 24th of August is from HQ UNCRO, Zagreb, and we see on the first page --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Haven't you got it on your screen, General Forand?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it is not from UNCRO, it is from my headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it from your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have got HQ UNCRO, Zagreb written on top of my document.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is from the headquarters Sector South to headquarters UNCRO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, it may be -- well, I know that this is a document that has been in the system several times over, and I have a version of it that comes out with that on top. So we'll ignore what is on my document. I'm sure it's got the same information. Can we go to the next page of the document. Your Honour, I'm trying to find because there's a document in different forms in the system which derails me. Can we see if I can have 65 ter 2477. Sorry about this. But, again, Your Honour, it is just a feature of the system which makes it difficult to manage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is the one that I have got, which has got HQ UNCRO Zagreb on it.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is what I was referring to, and it's the same date and I think even the same time as the one --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it appears to be me a different time. This one, I see, is 2403. PSAT 374 is an August 24th, 2030 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Yeah. Can we go to page 3 of this document. Thank you. Yes. That's the letter there from Colonel Tymchuk, which is the part that I was looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise this letter from Colonel Tymchuk?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
