utterances.text: The letter refers to: "If General Cermak is unable to proceed in this way, as we have agreed, then commander Sector South would like to be informed in writing of the position of the government of Croatia, so that the necessary higher level negotiations may begin to resolve this issue." Do you recollect that, concerning the manner in which the allegations of war crimes against individuals were going to be dealt with?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember is that they had some -- there was some discussion between myself, Al-Alfi, and General Cermak about the possibility that those that were not accused of being war criminal would be allowed to be sent to Serbia, and we would keep in the camp only those that were accused by the Croat of being war criminal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. Would it be right say that you, General Cermak, and Mr. Al-Alfi, and probably Mr. Flynn, were looking at ways of trying to solve this problem through different means?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if it was through different means. I know that we discussed it with General Cermak, because the problem I was having is trying to maintain the feeling of these people within my camp, which was creating a problem. So one way to alleviate that problem was to remove those people that were not considered war criminals. So we had started those discussion with General Cermak, which initially looked good but it didn't -- it didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D313, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D313 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, moving along through the documents, may we look at 65 ter 2467, which is Exhibit P374, which was the previous document of the 24th of August at 2030.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this is one of your sitreps. And if we just turn to page 3, paragraph 4, where you are writing on the issue of those that need to be considered, we see that the number is now 62 from 74 in paragraph 3. But it was the position in paragraph 4 that it was now clear that the matter could not be resolved at Sector South level. "It must be pursued between higher level in authorities and the government of Croatia." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what is written there, yes. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that goes back to what I was putting to you about Mr. Cermak acting on behalf of the government of Croatia. He didn't actually have the authority to conclude the matter under his own decisions.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The story of the matter continued over a number of days into September. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recollect that there was also an issue of the parties taking legal advice on the position within international law, as to where these people could be questioned and their manner of surrender?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware, through Mr. Al-Alfi that, yes, that matter was being discussed at a higher level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could go to a document, 65 ter 762, which is a report from Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan, and turn to page 3 of this report and look at paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This concerns you and General Cermak. And we can see about the context of the United Nations and that: "An issue has arisen as a result of a further oral agreement made on the 21st of August, 1995, between General Cermak, representing Croatia, and General Forand, on behalf of the United Nations, being disputed by the Croatian authorities." Do you recollect that you and General Cermak had actually agreed in an informal way how to resolve the matter some days earlier.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We thought, you know, that we had the -- an agreement that those people that were not accused of being war criminals could leave my camp to go to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And do you recollect that, in fact, Mr. Cermak was overruled by that, and what he had agreed with you was not accepted by the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think, not too long after that or during that period, either a meeting I had with General Cermak, with Mr. Al-Alfi, or a letter I received from him, indicated that it would not be so, that the agreement could not be -- could not be put into effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And do you recollect that, after that, that brought the Croatian government into the matter, trying to negotiate directly with the UN in relation to these people?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, except as I told you before, I was not involved in the dealing per se. It was Mr. Al-Alfi, and the direction was coming from UN Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May that be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the transcript reads "no objection," and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that's what I thought you would say. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D314, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D314 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm moving on through the account, which is it right to say that for several weeks, again, the dispute as to how to deal with the individuals continued until mid-September when it was resolved.

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I left, I think, on the 11th or 12 September to come back to Canada, and the issue was not resolved when I left for Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a number of documents in this matter which contain the full account, full story, which I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would there again be a possibility, perhaps, that this apparently is, of course we have not seen it yet, but the administrative follow-up of what the witness has described. Is there any way that we would give these documents to the witness, to invite him, not only to spoil his coffee breaks, but perhaps even part of the day, quickly scan through them, and see whether something is familiar to him or whether there's anything in it which he would like to comment on?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'll be frank. The crux of this evidence is really for the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- and fleshing out the whole picture which has been referred to, in part, in the Prosecution case. But we have been able to put together the entire narrative, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's all documents in relation to this, no statements by persons, but just the type of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Letters from Croatian government ministers, from the office of the president, taking over this matter from the hands of Mr. Cermak, and simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And most likely not ever have been to the knowledge of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could also limit. Of course, we'd like to receive all these documents in evidence, unless there is any objection against it. But, of course, if the witness -- I mean, my suggested way to proceed is not to spend time on matters on which the witness can't add anything to what is in the documents and, at the same time, that if the witness is in a position, if he has knowledge of the documents, to tell us what he knows about it. We could, for example, ask the witness to look at the documents and just report to us whether he has ever seen these documents before or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know he won't have, but it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can confess that is done for the knowledge of the Trial Chamber, and that is, in our view, a legitimate aim that we have in this case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- to present facts fully to you, as Your Honour said at the start of this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I just made the suggestion that in order to avoid that the witness would have some useful information on these documents and then not to miss that. But if you all expect that he doesn't have any specific knowledge about the documents, then let's just look at the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to go to the end of the story because we know that the people came out of the camp, and a number of people were taken to be interviewed under agreements reached between the Croatian government and the UN. Is that right, putting it in a summary?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I was told when I came back from Canada, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Should we just look at a document dated 18th of September, 1995, 2D03-0082.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Court may remember I asked the Colonel Leslie something about at the end of his examination, whether he recalled writing a particular document; and for the Court's assistance, this is the document that has now been found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have a review of the matter by Colonel Leslie in this document, which is an assessment. And in the second paragraph, it says: "The initial cooperation of the Croatian military appeared to be outstanding. Colonel General Cermak, military governor of Knin, friendly, helpful, when we met with him on Wednesday, the 14th of September, 1995, to discuss the movement plan, and he donated a truckload of clothing and arranged for food and juices for the displaced persons ... and the Croat police also appeared good ..." And this is an account of the transfer which, sadly, when it left Knin, was perhaps not so pleasant and there was trouble en route. But were you aware that the view of UNCRO was that Colonel-General Cermak had been outstanding in his cooperation to resolve this matter?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I was in Canada. I never saw that letter. I heard about the -- the problem that they had once they had left Knin. I don't remember the staff officer that briefed me, you know, raising praise of General Cermak, but it seemed to have gone well in Knin itself, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document go in as an exhibit. It was one, you will remember, I couldn't produce on my feet with Colonel Leslie.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D315, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the next matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would allow me to admit into evidence, Mr. Kay, it might be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm trying to finish a subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. D315 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Next document is 2D03-0101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you leave your microphone open, everyone can enjoy your short conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I need a remote control, and it would be easier, Your Honour, otherwise I might knock over some water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is within the competency of the registrar, not the Bench. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is the last document before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document from Colonel Karel Blahna, acting Sector South commander. This was written while you were in Canada?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It says: "Your Excellency, Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, on the 16th and 17th of September, the transfer the refugees was carried out in accordance with UNCRO and Sector South commander's plan." That would be your plan. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, even though I was not there, all the staff working for me, obviously I take the responsibility of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it refers to the particular transport of the inhabitants. In paragraph 2, it refers to the international organisations. One of the key persons of success of this mission was Colonel General Ivan Cermak and his liaison officers, Captain Lukovic, Lieutenant Mrsa, Ensign Dondo. Thanks to their initiative and responsible actions, this mission was done successfully. "Please, relay my personal gratitude and thanks to Colonel General Ivan Cermak for the quick and professional arrangements." Signed by Colonel Blahna, "job well done." Was that reported back to you?

utterances.speaker: ALAIN ROBERT FORAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but it -- I mean, it is there, it is signed, so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D316, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D316 is admitted into evidence. We have to adjourn for the day, Mr. Kay, but not before I have one question for you. You have described D312 as a list of 72 people who were those under discussion as to what the allegation was in relation to those people. May I ask you to consider whether this is a fair description of what a list is, especially in view of the word "allegation", and perhaps all lawyers in this courtroom listen fairly well, that apparently under number 35, the allegation just says "lawyer," of a person of almost 70 years old. I don't whether sometimes it is being the wife of or a relative of, so, whether these are really allegations or just clues to what apparently has raised whatever suspicion. We adjourn.
